questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Asking for the main idea
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a whole-text question from a single-slot question
questions.stem: A notice reads: « Les inscriptions au club de théâtre restent ouvertes jusqu'au 15 mars. » A reader is looking for the main idea. What kind of question is that reader asking?

options.text: which one statement the whole notice exists to deliver
which of the dates named in the notice matters least
options.misconception: inverts the question, asking for what is peripheral rather than central

options.text: how many separate facts the notice has packed into its lines
options.misconception: counts sentences and mistakes a total for a claim

options.text: which of the two clauses was drafted first by its author
options.misconception: asks about the writing process instead of the meaning

questions.explanation: A main-idea question asks for the single claim the rest of the text is there to support, and a text built from one claim is easy to summarise in a sentence. In this notice that claim is that registrations stay open until a given date, and the detail about which club and which month is what fills the claim out. The two questions that get confused with it are the counting question and the detail question, and both fail the same test: a detail can be answered by quoting one sentence, while a main idea cannot. The trap here is counting clauses, since a notice of three lines has three facts in it and only one point.
questions.hint: Ask whether the answer could be quoted from a single sentence alone.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Asking for a detail
questions.learningObjective: recognise a question that one sentence can answer
questions.stem: The same notice adds: « Les répétitions ont lieu le mardi à dix-huit heures. » A reader is now looking for a detail. What is the question?

options.text: which specific piece of information the notice gives on one point
what single claim the whole notice is meant to convey at once
options.misconception: asks for the main idea while thinking of one line

options.text: how the two clauses of the notice compare with each other
options.misconception: invents a comparison the text does not make

options.text: why the author chose this particular word in this line
options.misconception: turns a factual question into a question about word choice

questions.explanation: A detail question names one slot in the text and can be answered by pointing at a single sentence, which is exactly what this line is: when the rehearsals happen, and where. The main idea of the same notice is the closing date, and that has to be gathered from the whole piece rather than lifted from one line. The useful habit is to ask the two questions in that order, main idea first, because once the claim is known a detail can be checked against it and an irrelevant line is easy to spot. The trap is treating any one line as if it settled the piece, which is how a reader ends up summarising a schedule and calling it the point.
questions.hint: Ask whether the answer sits in one line of the text.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Reading for tone
questions.learningObjective: name the tone a short formula creates and the words that create it
questions.stem: A line reads: « Je comprends tout à fait votre inquiétude, et je reste à votre disposition. » What tone does that line take?

options.text: formal and reassuring, with a respectful distance kept in place
casual and hurried, as two people use who know each other well
options.misconception: reads a set phrase as the language of a close friend

options.text: sharp and accusing, with a fault left for the reader to find
options.misconception: finds an accusation where the line offers sympathy

options.text: doubtful and hesitant, as if the writer lacked solid facts
options.misconception: reads politeness as a mark of uncertainty about the facts

questions.explanation: Tone comes out of word choice rather than out of subject matter, and both halves of this line are set phrases that belong to a formal register: « je comprends tout à fait votre inquiétude » acknowledges the reader in the third person, and « je reste à votre disposition » offers help in a fixed formula used when a speaker stands slightly to one side. Nothing in the topic forces that register, which is the point, since the same concern can be raised as « j'ai bien compris que ça t'inquiète ». The trap is reading tone off the content, so a sympathetic subject makes a line sound warm even when its wording is stiff and distant.
questions.hint: Ask which pronoun the writer uses for the person being addressed.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Attitude and the evidence offered for it
questions.learningObjective: separate a stated opinion from the observations behind it
questions.stem: A review says: « Ce roman se lit d'une traite, et l'auteur n'a évidemment rien laissé au hasard. » What is the review giving as evidence for its attitude?

options.text: the speed of the book and the care credited to its author
the number of chapters and the size of the printed volume
options.misconception: takes physical facts as though they carried the praise

options.text: the price of the book and the size of its first printing
options.misconception: reaches for market facts the review never mentions at all

options.text: the titles of two other books by writers of the same period
options.misconception: assumes a comparison was made when none is stated

questions.explanation: The attitude here is admiration, and the review backs it with two observations rather than with the admiration itself. « Se lit d'une traite » is a remark about pace, and « rien laissé au hasard » credits deliberate craft, so each half of the praise has something behind it. What is not evidence is the verdict, because « c'est un bon livre » supports itself and adds nothing. The trap is to gather anything factual-sounding that sits near a verdict and call it a reason, and it is worth noticing that neither chapter count nor price appears anywhere in the sentence.
questions.hint: Ask which clauses describe the book rather than praise it.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Purpose and how a writer signals it
questions.learningObjective: find the sentence that names both genre and intention
questions.stem: A text begins: « Dans cet essai, je propose une autre lecture de ce roman. » How has the writer signalled the purpose of the piece?

options.text: by naming the kind of text and the intention in the first line
by quoting three separate passages before making any claim
options.misconception: believes a purpose has to be delayed behind quotations

options.text: by naming every writer who argued the same thing before
options.misconception: looks for a survey of sources as the sign of purpose

options.text: by setting a question for the reader to answer in the opening line
options.misconception: confuses an invitation to think with a statement of aim

questions.explanation: Two pieces of information sit in that opening: « dans cet essai » names what kind of piece this is, and « je propose » names what the writer intends to do inside it. Together they tell a reader what to expect for the rest of the text, which is what a purpose sentence is for. The other signals are real techniques but they are not this one, since a quotation supports an argument rather than announcing it, and a list of predecessors belongs to a later paragraph at the earliest. The trap is looking for the purpose only at the end, where writers also state it, and missing the announcement that the first line has already made.
questions.hint: Ask which two pieces of information the first line carries.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The move an argument makes
questions.learningObjective: describe what a reframing sentence shifts and what it keeps
questions.stem: A writer argues: « Ce n'est pas le livre qu'on ne lit plus, c'est qu'on ne prend plus le temps de s'arrêter. » What is the sentence doing?

options.text: moving the cause of lost reading from the books to the time
denying outright that reading habits have changed in recent years
options.misconception: reads a correction as a denial of any change at all

options.text: claiming that people now read more books than they once read
options.misconception: inverts the claim and makes it a claim about an increase

options.text: insisting that reading rooms ought to be closed rather than opened
options.misconception: imports a policy proposal the sentence never makes

questions.explanation: The shape « ce n'est pas X, c'est Y » takes an explanation that is already in circulation and swaps in a better one, and the swap is between a thing blamed and a habit blamed. Books stay in the sentence, so the writer is not denying that reading has changed; the writer is saying the cause sits somewhere else, in time rather than in titles. That makes it an argument rather than a piece of description, and it is also what makes it vulnerable, since a reader can accept the framing and still dispute the cause. The trap is hearing the first half as a cancellation of everything that came before it.
questions.hint: Ask what the second half replaces rather than denies.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A claim the text has not supported
questions.learningObjective: identify what is missing when a figure is offered bare
questions.stem: A short article says: « Un quart des élèves du quartier abandonne la lecture au bout de six mois. » What has the article not yet supplied?

options.text: the source of the figure and the way it was actually counted
the names of the schools and the dates of the school terms
options.misconception: asks for administrative detail the claim never rested on

options.text: the ages of the pupils and the length of each school day
options.misconception: looks for background facts instead of the missing support

options.text: the titles of the books read and the price paid for them
options.misconception: wants particulars about the reading rather than about the count

questions.explanation: A figure is a claim, not a piece of evidence, and until the article says where the quarter came from and how the six months were counted, the sentence can be checked against nothing. Specificity is not support: writing a proportion rather than the word « many » makes the sentence sound firmer without making it any better founded, which is exactly how a bare number persuades. The useful test is to ask what a reader would need in order to repeat the count, and the answer here names a source and a method. The trap is asking for the interesting details of the subject instead of the machinery behind the number.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would need in order to check the figure.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: An inference that follows and one that does not
questions.learningObjective: keep an inference inside what the text licenses
questions.stem: A text says: « La bibliothèque ouvre à neuf heures et ferme à dix-huit heures. Elle était vide mardi. » Which reading follows from those two lines?

options.text: the library was quiet on Tuesday, whatever the reason for it
Tuesday was the busiest day of the week for that library
options.misconception: reverses a stated fact into the opposite of what it says

options.text: the opening hours were changed on Tuesday to suit the staff
options.misconception: invents a change of schedule the text never mentions

options.text: no visitor came on Tuesday because the weather was poor
options.misconception: supplies a cause that the text leaves entirely unstated

questions.explanation: An inference is licensed when the text would be hard to explain without it, and a quiet Tuesday inside stated opening hours is exactly that. What the text does not do is say why, so the inference stops at the emptiness and the reason stays open; the phrasing that keeps the reason open is what makes the reading a reading rather than a report. The three rejected readings each add something the sentences never contain, and the fourth is the commonest, because readers supply a weather explanation and then quote the sentence as though it had said it. An inference with a cause in it is usually a guess wearing an inference's clothes.
questions.hint: Ask whether the second sentence could be explained some other way.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Bias carried by a single word
questions.learningObjective: spot a distancing marker and say what it signals
questions.stem: A columnist writes: « La fameuse réforme n'a encore produit aucun résultat. » Which word shows where the writer stands?

options.text: « fameuse », held at a distance by the quotation marks round it
« réforme », which names the measure in neutral official words
options.misconception: treats a technical label as though it carried judgement

options.text: « encore », which counts how many times the reform has run
options.misconception: hears a frequency in a word that marks recurrence only

options.text: « aucun », which quotes a figure from an official statement
options.misconception: supposes a citation where no source has been given

questions.explanation: Guillemets around a plain word like « fameuse » are a distancing device, and what they signal is that the writer is repeating a description without owning it, often with a barb attached. The word itself is praise, and the marks turn the praise into something the writer is quoting in order to set aside. The rest of the sentence then confirms the stance, since a reform that has produced nothing is a complaint dressed as a report. The trap is reading the quotation marks as though something were actually being cited, because in French they mark a term chosen by somebody else, not a quotation from a source.
questions.hint: Ask which word is praised and then held at arm's length.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Euphemism and what it covers
questions.learningObjective: give the plain statement a softened phrase is standing in for
questions.stem: An official letter says: « Nous avons procédé à un redéploiement des effectifs. » What is that phrase covering up?

options.text: the fact that posts have been cut and staff let go
the fact that the offices have moved to a new building
options.misconception: hears a change of place inside a word about staff

options.text: the fact that new working hours have been put in place
options.misconception: reads a personnel measure as a change of timetable

options.text: the fact that the staff were given extra training last year
options.misconception: inverts the direction of a staffing measure entirely

questions.explanation: « Effectifs » means the people an organisation employs, and « redéploiement » means sending them somewhere else, which together stand in for posts being cut and people being let go. A euphemism is not a lie; it is a true phrase chosen because the plainer one is unpleasant, and the effect is that a decision arrives sounding like an adjustment. Reading the letter properly means giving the sentence back its plain meaning and then deciding how to answer it. The trap is taking the word at the level of the letter, where a redeployment sounds like a promotion and nothing in the vocabulary says otherwise.
questions.hint: Ask what an organisation is actually short of when posts are cut.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Hyperbole and what it intensifies
questions.learningObjective: say what an exaggeration enlarges and what it cannot report
questions.stem: A cook writes: « La file d'attente faisait le tour de la place et les assiettes n'arrivaient plus. » What does the exaggeration enlarge?

options.text: how long and how bad the wait grew, not its measured length
how many people waited, counted exactly as it is written
options.misconception: reads an enlarged figure as a number worth quoting

options.text: how much the cooking improved since the restaurant opened
options.misconception: turns a complaint about service into praise for the food

options.text: how quickly the queue moved once it began moving at all
options.misconception: infers a speed from a line that reports a standstill

questions.explanation: A queue that goes round a square is not a measurement, it is a way of saying the wait was far too long, and the second clause about the plates adds the sense that service had stopped entirely. Hyperbole enlarges in the direction the writer feels, so it is a reliable sign of feeling and an unreliable sign of scale. That is the practical reason to name it when summarising, since a reader who reports the size of the queue back as a fact has changed the kind of claim on the page. The trap is treating the number of details in a hyperbole as though more detail meant more accuracy.
questions.hint: Ask whether the shape of the queue could have been measured.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Idiom against literal reading
questions.learningObjective: give the idiomatic sense in place of the literal one
questions.stem: A colleague says: « Ce rapport, il ne tourne pas rond. » What is the speaker actually reporting?

options.text: that the report has a serious fault somewhere in its reasoning
that the report has been printed on the wrong kind of paper
options.misconception: takes the image of a wheel as though it were about printing

options.text: that the report came back from the printer much later than due
options.misconception: reads a complaint about quality as one about delivery

options.text: that nobody has yet given the report a first careful reading
options.misconception: supposes a stage of handling rather than a fault in the work

questions.explanation: « Ne pas tourner rond » belongs to the family of expressions about machines that are not running properly, and applied to a piece of writing it means the working is faulty rather than the machine. Idioms carry a meaning that the words do not add up to, and that is why the figurative sense has to be stored whole: there is no way to derive it from the parts. French is rich in this family, with « mettre les points sur les i » and « être sur le point » sitting right beside it, and each has to be learnt as a unit. The trap is building the meaning out of the words, which is how a learner ends up with a complaint about printing.
questions.hint: Ask what a machine does when it is not working properly.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Words that mark a register
questions.learningObjective: pick out the two words that set a familiar tone
questions.stem: A message reads: « Salut ! On se voit demain à midi, ça te va ? » Which two words carry the register of that message?

options.text: « Salut » and « ça te va », both used between people on familiar terms
« On se voit », which is a formula reserved for written notices
options.misconception: claims a set phrase for the written form only

options.text: « demain » and « à midi », which belong to a business appointment
options.misconception: reads a time expression as a marker of register

options.text: « à » and « te », which never appear in a spoken message
options.misconception: calls two everyday words formal markers on no evidence

questions.explanation: Register markers are words rather than topics, and the two here both belong to the spoken language used between people who know each other. « Salut » is a greeting that would be out of place in a letter to a stranger, and « ça te va » is the contraction of « est-ce que cela te convient », a phrase that has been worn down by use until the formal version has gone. « On se voit » is neutral rather than informal, since it appears in appointments as well, and a time expression carries no register at all. The trap is looking for markers in the subject matter, when a friendly plan and a business appointment can be worded in exactly the same register.
questions.hint: Ask which two words would be out of place in a formal letter.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A formal register against an informal one
questions.learningObjective: say which features separate two ways of asking the same thing
questions.stem: Two notes are compared: « Veuillez me confirmer votre présence avant le 3 mai. » and « Peux-tu me dire si tu viens le 3 ? » What separates them?

options.text: the vous form and a set phrase in the first, a direct tu form in the second
a full date in the first and only a day of the week in the second
options.misconception: reads a naming practice as though it carried the register

options.text: three more words in the first than there are in the second
options.misconception: judges register by length instead of by wording

options.text: a question about attendance in the first and one about travel in the second
options.misconception: claims a difference of subject that the two notes do not have

questions.explanation: Both notes ask the same practical question and both name a date, so the difference is in the wording rather than in the content. « Veuillez me confirmer votre présence » uses the polite imperative with « vous » and a noun in the third person, which is what an office produces; « Peux-tu me dire si tu viens » uses the tu form, a contracted verb and a short clause, which is what two people who know each other produce. The trap is that register is often mistaken for length, and a long sentence can be just as informal as a short one. What marks the level is the choice of pronoun and of set phrase, both of which are visible here.
questions.hint: Ask which pronoun of address each note uses.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A pun and the sound it turns on
questions.learningObjective: name the two words a pun leans on and what each means
questions.stem: A garden centre's sign reads: « Un jardin sans vers n'est pas un jardin vert. » What is the sign doing there?

options.text: leaning on two words that sound alike, vers and vert, and differ in sense
contrasting the soil to use with the grass that will grow in it
options.misconception: reads a plain instruction as though it hid a device

options.text: advertising a book on gardening written by two different authors
options.misconception: supposes a title is named when no title is present

options.text: warning visitors about a pest found in one bed of the nursery
options.misconception: takes the practical sense and misses the sound

questions.explanation: « Vers » and « vert » are pronounced the same, and the sign is built on the fact that a garden without worms is not a green one. That is the whole mechanism of a pun: one sound, two senses, and a sentence that means both at once, which is why a pun cannot be translated word for word without losing the joke. French has a good stock of these, and they turn most often on short pairs like « gare » and « war », so learning them is a matter of ears as much as of words. The trap is reading the sign as practical advice, which is a perfectly reasonable reading of the sense and misses the effect entirely.
questions.hint: Ask what the two words ending the line have in common.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Alliteration and its effect
questions.learningObjective: name the repeated sound and the speed it produces
questions.stem: An opening line runs: « Le vent vif vendait du vin vert. » What is the line doing with its sounds?

options.text: repeating one consonant so the words seem to race past together
repeating one vowel so the line slows down to a full stop
options.misconception: confuses the repeated consonant with a repeated vowel

options.text: repeating a whole syllable so the line becomes a proverb
options.misconception: hears a proverb where the repetition is only a sound

options.text: repeating a long vowel so the line ends on an open question
options.misconception: takes a sound pattern for a grammatical mood

questions.explanation: The line repeats a single consonant at the start of each word, which is what alliteration is, and the effect follows from the friction: a string of hard consonants makes the reader move quickly, so the line suits what it describes. The words chosen also fit, since a keen wind selling green wine is nonsense taken straight, and the nonsense is the point of a line written for sound. The trap is mixing the families, because a repeated vowel is a different figure and a repeated syllable is a third, and naming the right one is what tells a reader why the line works.
questions.hint: Ask which letter the line keeps giving back to the ear.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Anaphora and its effect
questions.learningObjective: describe what a repeated opening does to a list of demands
questions.stem: A petition closes: « Nous voulons des délais, nous voulons des explications, nous voulons des preuves. » What is the repetition doing?

options.text: fixing one opening on three clauses so the demand gathers weight
varying each opening so the list reads as a fair balance
options.misconception: says the opposite of what a repeated opening does

options.text: closing every clause the same way so the tone turns formal
options.misconception: moves the device from the openings to the endings

options.text: repeating one noun so the reader can count what is asked for
options.misconception: treats a repeated clause as though it repeated a single noun

questions.explanation: « Nous voulons » opens all three clauses, and that is anaphora: the same beginning, three times, with the object changing each time. The effect is cumulative rather than informative, since the reader is not learning three separate things but three terms of the same demand, and the rhythm stops each one before the next begins. Writers reach for it at the end of a text precisely because it produces pressure without adding a fact. The trap is to read a repeated opening as a way of varying the list, when varying would defeat the purpose of repeating.
questions.hint: Ask which words open each of the three clauses.

questions.topic: Screening for figures of speech
questions.learningObjective: keep the three lines that use a figure and reject the plain one
questions.stem: A reviewer offers four short lines. Three of them use a figure of speech, and one is plain reporting. Which is the plain one?

options.text: « La salle tremblait sous les applaudissements »
options.misconception: reads a plain report where the line is working as a figure

options.text: « Le temps fuit sans bruit »
options.misconception: misses that a human verb has been given to time

options.text: « La ville dort sous la pluie fine »
options.misconception: misses a figure where a place is given a human sleep

options.text: « Il a ouvert la porte et il est entré »

The other three each give something a thing cannot literally do: a room does not tremble under applause, time does not run, and a city does not sleep. Naming what has been given to what is the quickest way to see this, because in each of the three the verb or the action belongs to a person and has been handed to something else. The trap is to expect a figure in every short line, which is how a plain sentence gets praised for a device it does not have.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Teaching the search for a main idea
questions.learningObjective: give a three-step method and apply it to a notice
questions.stem: A learner asks how to find the main idea of a text they have just read. Explain the method you would teach and show it working on a short notice you write yourself.

answer.exemplar: I would teach three steps. First, read for the claim: ask what the writer wants a reader to think, and look for a sentence that could be sent on by itself. Second, test every other sentence against it: if a line does not support, explain or exemplify that claim, it is decoration and can be set aside. Third, rewrite the claim in your own words and check that no essential part of the text has been lost. On a notice reading « Les lectures du soir commencent le 8 janvier. Les laissez-passer sont délivrés à l'accueil. Les salles ferment à vingt heures », the claim is when the sessions begin, the second line tells the reader how to get in, and the third is a detail, so the summary is one sentence and not three.

questions.explanation: Learners tend to summarise a text by listing its sentences, and the reason they do is that nobody has shown them the test that separates a claim from a detail. The second step is the one that carries the weight, since a line that supports nothing can be discarded without loss, and a line that exemplifies the claim is still part of the claim. Asking for a one-sentence version is a good discipline because it forces a choice, and the choice is exactly what a summary is. The failure to watch for is the sentence that sounds important and supports nothing, such as a piece of background the writer found interesting.
questions.hint: Ask which lines would be missed if the summary were cut short.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Teaching how tone is worked out from wording
questions.learningObjective: give a method for reading tone out of word choice
questions.stem: A learner asks how the tone of a message can be worked out from its wording. Explain the method you would teach and apply it to three sentences they have written.

answer.exemplar: I would teach three checks, all of them on wording rather than subject. Look at the pronoun of address, since « vous » and the tu form mark distance and closeness on their own. Look for set phrases, since « je reste à votre disposition » and « à bientôt » both come from registers and a mixed set gives a mixed tone. Then look at the length and shape of the sentences, since a long subordinate opening sounds careful and a clipped one sounds brisk or short-tempered. On « Je vous remercie de votre retour, qui me convient tout à fait », all three agree on a formal and courteous note. On « C'est noté, on fait comme ça », all three agree on something brisk, and the subject being the same makes the difference plain.

questions.explanation: Tone is often treated as a mood that a reader simply feels, which leaves a learner unable to justify an answer or to control one in their own writing. The three checks turn it into evidence: the pronoun says how the writer stands to the reader, the set phrase says which world the sentence comes from, and the sentence shape says how much care went into it. Read together they also explain mixed cases, since a courteous pronoun inside a clipped sentence produces a tone that is polite and impatient at once. That is a useful result, because it shows a writer how to change one register marker without rewriting the whole message.
questions.hint: Ask which pronoun, which set phrase and which sentence shape are present.

questions.topic: Chiasmus and the order it turns on
questions.learningObjective: spot a balanced reversal and the contrast it builds
questions.stem: A writer says: « Il avait faim de mots, puis il a mangé ses mots. » What is that line built on?

questions.topic: Building a thesis with three criteria
questions.learningObjective: state a claim and three tests it can be argued against
questions.stem: A learner asks how to write a thesis that can actually be argued for. Explain your method and build one thesis of your own with three criteria attached.

answer.exemplar: I would teach three requirements. The thesis must be arguable, so a reader could disagree with it; it must be specific, so it names a group and a situation rather than saying that something is good or bad; and it must be limited, so the ground it covers is ground a short piece can actually cover. Then I attach three criteria, which are simply the three questions the argument will answer. A thesis that works: the reading corners in our school are not failing for want of books but for want of scheduled time. The three criteria behind it are the presence of the books, the presence of a slot in the timetable, and the presence of an adult in the room, and each of the three can be argued for on evidence somebody could go and look at.

questions.explanation: Most weak theses fail on the first requirement without the writer knowing, because a statement nobody can disagree with cannot be argued for either. Arguability is therefore the test to apply first, and specificity is what makes a disagreement possible, since a claim about everybody cannot be met with a counter-example from one street. The third requirement, a limit on the ground covered, is what stops a short piece from promising to settle a question it can only open. Naming three criteria after the thesis is useful for a second reason: it shows in advance whether the evidence is going to be there, and a writer who cannot list three is usually trying to argue for something there is no evidence about.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reader could disagree with the claim you have written.

answer.exemplar: A conclusion repeats the introduction when it says the same claim in the same words, and the reader recognises it as a loop because nothing has been added since the first paragraph. What a conclusion should add is one of three things: a consequence the reader has not been given, a limit on the claim that was made, or a step that now looks obvious and did not at the start. Take an essay on reading corners that opens by saying the school should keep its reading corner. A conclusion that repeats would close by saying the school should keep its reading corner. One that adds would close by naming the three conditions under which that is true, and by admitting that without a volunteer in the room on Thursdays the argument does not hold. That limit is what makes the ending worth reading.

Restating is a job for a summary, and a summary is not what a last paragraph is for, so the repetition is read as a sign that the writer has run out. The three things that do work are all forward-looking: a consequence pushes the argument out into the world, a limit admits what the argument cannot cover, and a newly visible step shows the reader how far the thinking has travelled. The limit is the one beginners leave out, and it is the one that earns trust, since an argument that admits its own edge is easier to believe than one that claims everything.

The second is the difference in what each line assumes about the reader, since one expects a reader who will notice a sound and the other a reader who will notice a sky. The third is the difference in what each account makes of the same building, because emptiness can be read as a disappointment or as a relief. Once the subject is held constant, each writer's selection becomes visible, and selection is the part of writing that a reader cannot normally see in a single text. The second gain is the clearest one: two accounts of the same place show what each writer expected the reader to notice, which is a fact about the writer rather than about the place. questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Teaching the test for a supported claim
questions.learningObjective: give a way of checking support and apply it to two claims
questions.stem: A learner asks how to tell whether a claim on a page is actually supported. Explain the test you would teach and apply it to two claims they write.

answer.exemplar: I would teach one test and one habit. The test is the repeat test: could somebody else go and do the same check, with the same words, and get the same result? A claim about a quarter of the pupils failing at reading passes only if the page says where the quarter came from and how it was counted. The habit is to mark the support next to the claim, in a phrase rather than a page number, so a reader can see at a glance whether the two belong together. On « Les élèves mangent mal parce qu'ils ont une demi-heure », the claim about the cause has nothing beside it, since no count, date or comparison is offered, and the sentence is a worry rather than a finding. On « Il y a eu douze absences en janvier contre vingt-six en octobre », the claim is supported, because the figures and the comparison are both on the page.

questions.explanation: Learners rarely set out to write unsupported claims; they write claims they believe and then stop, so the useful thing to teach is a check they can run afterwards rather than a rule to remember in advance. The repeat test works because support has to be reproducible, and a memory of something true is not. Pairing the test with the habit of marking support beside the claim catches the second failure as well, which is the mismatch of a real figure to the wrong claim, something a careful reader will not notice because the figure is there. Both together turn support into something visible on the page instead of something the writer assumes.
questions.hint: Ask whether another reader could repeat the check that produced the claim.

The sentence about taking books home is not lost either, since it is part of what readers have to do rather than background. Every omission is a claim that the line carried no necessary information, and a writer who cannot defend one of those claims has summarised too little.

A summary is a series of judgements, and each removed line is a judgement that it added nothing a reader needs. What the tone rules out is any warmth towards whoever caused it, and also any accusation, since a sentence that accuses needs a sharper word than « je note ». The set phrases do most of the work here, and « pour mémoire » in particular pulls the sentence towards the language of a committee, which is why a reader hears a formality that the bare fact would not carry. The permitted attitude is narrow, and saying what the tone rules out is what stops a reading answer from sliding into a judgement the page never made. It is a small skill, but it is the one that separates a reader from an opinion about a reader.

questions.topic: Translating to a client and then to a friend
questions.learningObjective: hold a register and then change it deliberately
questions.stem: Stage one: translate « Could you have this ready by Friday? » into French at the same level of politeness. Stage two: say what would change if the reader were a friend rather than a client.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: « Pourriez-vous avoir cela prêt pour vendredi ? » keeps the level, because the conditional is the French device for a courteous request and « pourriez-vous » is the standard form with a stranger whose co-operation is wanted. Stage two: the friend version is « Tu pourrais me faire ça pour vendredi ? », and three things change at once. The pronoun of address moves from « vous » to « tu », the request becomes a question the friend can refuse without any ceremony, and the object becomes « ça », a neutral word that costs nothing. Nothing about the deadline is softer and nothing about the request is stronger, so the transaction is identical and only the footing has moved. That is the useful lesson: register is not politeness added to content, it is part of what the content is being said for.

questions.explanation: Translating the same sentence twice for two different readers is the clearest demonstration that register is a choice rather than a decoration, because everything except the footing stays exactly where it was. The three things that move in French are the pronoun, the frame of the request, and the vocabulary of the thing being asked for, and all three follow from the relationship rather than from politeness in general. Learners often stop at the pronoun and miss the rest, which is why a translated line can sound correctly polite and still be wrong for the reader. The deadline is worth holding steady in both versions, since softening the date as well as the wording would change the transaction rather than the tone.
